newsitem.title: USA: With kids flabby, pee-wee health a booming market.
newsitem.headline: With kids flabby, pee-wee health a booming market.

text.p: The statistics are all too familiar. Unlike their parents, who walked to school, attended daily gym classes and played outside until dark, the children of baby boomers are sadly out of shape.

According to a recent U.S. Surgeon General's Report on Physical Activity and Health, half of all kids between 12 and 21 are not physically active on a regular basis. According to the American Heart Association, at least 4 million American children have high blood pressure, a third are obese and 27 million have high cholesterol.
Walking to school and playing outdoors have become the exception, not the rule, amid fears of urban violence, drive-by shootings and child abductions.
New technology has kids sitting inside after school watching television and playing with computers, and when they do so they are munching chips, candy and other junk foods.

Gym class is also often a thing of the past, as nearly two-thirds of the nation's elementary and secondary schools -- many of them low on space and lower on funding -- have cut daily physical education classes, according to the American Heart Association.

"There's evidence that kids are even less physically active than in the past. I see no cause for optimism," said Dr. Lyle Micheli, director of sports medicine at Boston's Children's Hospital. "Everything would lead me to believe athletic kids are getting athletics and non-athletic kids getting nothing but junk food."
Unless a child is a competitive athlete, parents and school officials must seek out ways to interest children in health and fitness, Micheli said.
But what daunts parents and doctors is a boom to marketers, who have seen an entire kiddie fitness industry grow up in the past few years. It is a business worth millions -- and growing.

Health and fitness clubs have been opened, exercise videos have been shot and a rash of special exercise events and programmes, both non-profit and for-profit, have been designed specifically to appeal to children.

Discovery Zone, the indoor play centre company, touts studies showing that time spent in its shops contributes to childhood health. The shoe giant Nike Inc. touts its "P.L.A.Y. Programme," (Participating in the Lives of America's Youth), using sports stars like decathlete Dan O'Brien to convince kids to become physically fit and active, presumably while wearing the company's clothing.

Cardio Express Inc., a children's fitness video company in Orlando, sold 15,000 copies of its first children's exercise video its first week of release five years ago, said Randy Ross, the company's president.
"Because of television and video games, kids these days are very entertainment oriented. We try to make sure the workouts we put together have a strong entertainment edge," he said.
In September, the company started its second kids' exercise video, filming it with 4,500 area children at Universal Studios Florida, one of the area's theme parks.
The filming was in conjunction with one of the leading non-profit youth fitness programmes -- the "Inner City Games" designed by actor and former body builder Arnold Schwarzenegger.

"Kids think it's too hot to exercise and they think they are not going to get in shape anyway," said Emily Howell, 9, of Orlando, whose essay on fitness won her the chance to be a demonstrator in the video. "I wanted kids to know you can have fun and exercise at the same time."

Health clubs -- the beloved exercise bastion for baby boomers -- have offered babysitting for years. Some recently have begun to add children's exercise classes to their step, high-impact and low-impact offerings for adults.

At a conference this year, San Diego, Calif.-based IDEA, one of the world's largest fitness professional organisations, offered specific seminars on children's fitness programming. IDEA said that children like to exercise in health clubs because it makes them feel important.

"Kids want to have fun. They don't just want to exercise," said April Durrett, senior editor of IDEA Today magazine. "They might get bored of a step (aerobics) class in 6 weeks and not want to come back. If you put exercise under the auspices of a club, it's cool."
